# The field guide

Every kind of file this pipeline has met, what it is for in a university, and how to handle it.

**Generated from `formats/registry.json`. Do not edit this file.** Add an entry there, with the
document that showed it, and regenerate with:

```bash
node scripts/identify.mjs --write-guide
```

Drawn from a census of 2,325 files on 2026-09-14: 248 Word documents, 134 course summaries, 15,546 equations.

To ask what a file in front of you is:

```bash
node scripts/identify.mjs <file-or-folder> --all
```

## Handled

### Word, written in Word

<a id="word-native"></a>

**What it is for.** The ordinary summary. Somebody wrote it in Word and used the heading styles, so the document carries its own structure.

**How to handle it.** open-docx.js, then docx.js. The heading level is read from the style's outlineLvl, which is Word's own answer and does not depend on what the style is called.

**What goes wrong.** The generator is what makes this claim honest. Word ALWAYS writes <Application> into docProps/app.xml, so a document with headings and no generator was written somewhere else and belongs to google-docs-export instead.

**Seen.** 215 of 248 Word documents name Microsoft Office Word as their generator. SUMMARY_Introduction_to_Math: 1,615 paragraphs, 146 headings, 1,249 equations.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `headingStyles >0`, `generator ~Word`

### Word whose styles are named in another language

<a id="word-localised-styles"></a>

**What it is for.** The author's Word is not in English, so its built-in styles are not either. Nothing about the content is unusual, and the author has no idea anything is different.

**How to handle it.** Nothing special, because the level never comes from the name. A style carries outlineLvl in its own definition or inherits it through basedOn, and that is what makes it a heading.

**What goes wrong.** A rule that looks for a style called Heading finds nothing here and concludes the document is unstructured. The old extractor found 0 headings in Draft Summary; reading outlineLvl finds 18.

**Seen.** Draft Summary.docx: heading styles Cmsor1 to Cmsor7, which is Word writing the Hungarian Cimsor with the accents stripped out of the id. Accounting_Formula_Sheet: Egyenlet (equation) and Stlus3, Stlus4 (style).

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `accentStrippedStyles >0`

### Word carrying real equations

<a id="word-with-omml"></a>

**What it is for.** Any quantitative course. The equations are OOXML maths objects, not text, so they are invisible to anything that reads runs.

**How to handle it.** omml.js, reached through docx.js, then katex-check.js before a manifest exists.

**What goes wrong.** mammoth and python-docx drop <m:oMath> in SILENCE. The document comes out looking clean and missing every formula. This is the most expensive failure in the whole intake, because nothing about the result looks wrong.

**Seen.** 87 of 248 Word documents. 15,546 equations across the 134 summaries; one document holds 1,249.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `oMath >0`

### Word with a web page pasted into it

<a id="word-html-paste"></a>

**What it is for.** An author copied from a rendered page (a wiki, a lecture site, a maths page) straight into Word. The paste brings the page's CSS classes with it as Word styles.

**How to handle it.** Converts normally. The tell is a styles.xml full of names no author chose.

**What goes wrong.** Maths that was pasted as RENDERED HTML is not an equation any more; it is styled text that looks right and carries no <m:oMath>. Check the equation count against what the document appears to contain: these four had OMML as well, so the paste was not the whole document, but a document where oMath is 0 and the pages are full of formulas has lost every one of them.

**Seen.** Four accounting summaries carry KaTeX's own class names as Word styles: katex, base, strut, mord, msupsub, vlist, alongside msonormal0 from an HTML paste.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `htmlPasteStyles >0`

### Word written on the house template

<a id="word-semantic-template"></a>

**What it is for.** The summary template gives the author named styles for the things a summary is made of, so the author has already said which paragraph is an example, which is a recap, and which is not their prose at all.

**How to handle it.** Convert normally. `docx.js` writes each one into the Markdown as `<!-- style: In Short -->` above its paragraph, and the layout phase reads those instead of guessing. What a name may BECOME on the page is the platform's vocabulary: ask content_guide, never a list kept here.

**What goes wrong.** This is the one piece of authorial intent in the whole file and every extractor that asked only whether a style is a heading threw it away. Word marks these itself with w:customStyle="1", so finding them needs no list of names to keep up to date.

**Seen.** SUMMARY_Micro carries 37 marked paragraphs: Example (18), In Short (18) and not-prose (1). CHEAT_SHEET_Applied_Statistics adds Summary. GG_SummaryTemplate2026.dotx is the template itself.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `semanticStyles >0`

### A Word template, not a document

<a id="word-template"></a>

**What it is for.** The house format itself: the styles every summary is written on. It is what a new summary starts from, and it is not course content.

**How to handle it.** Never a source. Read it to learn what the house styles MEAN, which is what makes word-semantic-template readable.

**What goes wrong.** It parses perfectly and produces a document of placeholder text. Nothing about the output says it was a template.

**Seen.** GG_SummaryTemplate2026.dotx, GG_Template2025.docx

**Recognised by.** `ext = .dotx`

### Word that is still being reviewed

<a id="word-under-review"></a>

**What it is for.** A draft somebody has commented on. The comments are a conversation about the text, not part of it.

**How to handle it.** Converts normally and the comments do not come with it, because they live in a separate part. Treat the document as a DRAFT: somebody is still arguing with it.

**What goes wrong.** Nothing in the extracted text says the document was still being argued over, so a course can be built from a draft nobody signed off.

**Seen.** 24 of 248 Word documents carry word/comments.xml, including all seven Week N.docx files of one course.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `comments >0`

### Word with pictures, text boxes and drawn shapes

<a id="word-pictures-in-headings"></a>

**What it is for.** An author pasted a graph into a heading, or floated a label over the text. Ordinary authoring, and invisible in the text stream.

**How to handle it.** One ordered pass over the document, never a walk over paragraph-shaped chunks.

**What goes wrong.** A paragraph-based scan found 32 of those 53 pictures, 0 of the 10 text boxes and 3 of the 16 shapes. A text box and a drawn shape are the two defects no text diff can see.

**Seen.** 30 of 248 documents carry text boxes and 40 carry VML shapes. SUMMARY_Introduction_to_Math: 53 pictures, 10 text boxes, 16 shapes.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `textboxes >0`

### Word's HD Photo sidecars

<a id="wdp-sidecar"></a>

**What it is for.** None for us. Word writes an alternate-format copy beside each real picture.

**How to handle it.** Excluded from the media inventory. They are never content.

**What goes wrong.** Counting them reported 66 unreferenced images and buried the 2 that were genuinely orphaned.

**Seen.** 35 of 248 documents. 45 of the 98 media files in SUMMARY_Introduction_to_Math.

**Recognised by.** `wdp >0`

### A cheat sheet

<a id="cheat-sheet"></a>

**What it is for.** A one-page formula reference a student revises from. Almost all symbols, almost no prose, and one of the most useful things a course holds.

**How to handle it.** Converts normally. Its shape means the usual assumptions do not hold: it is not a lecture, it has no sections worth the name, and its density is the point.

**What goes wrong.** A word-count rule that decides a document is too thin rejects exactly these, and a no-headings rule flags them as broken when they are simply a list. The length is part of the identity: a 12,000-word summary with dense maths is a maths course, not a cheat sheet, and only the word count separates the two.

**Seen.** 10 of 248 documents. CHEAT_SHEET Applied Statistics: 530 words carrying 89 equations.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `oMath >20`, `wordsPerEquation <10`, `words <1500`

### Word where the equations are spreadsheet formulas

<a id="spreadsheet-formulas-as-equations"></a>

**What it is for.** A data or analytics course teaching Excel. The author typed the formulas into Word's equation editor because that is where formulas go.

**How to handle it.** Converts, but these are not mathematics and should not become formula blocks. They are code, and a code span reads better than a refused equation.

**What goes wrong.** An underscore inside a function name is a LaTeX escape problem and a dollar in a cell reference is a delimiter problem. Both refused equations before they were fixed.

**Seen.** 4 of 248 documents. Introduction to Data Analytics: SUMIF, SUMIFS, ROUND, IF among 100 equations.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `excelFormulas >0`

### A summary about money

<a id="money-summary"></a>

**What it is for.** Accounting, finance, operations. Prose full of amounts, and amounts inside the equations too.

**How to handle it.** Converts normally. The currency in prose is prose; the currency inside an equation is written as an escaped dollar.

**What goes wrong.** This one shape caused five separate bugs. A dollar in prose pairs with the next one and everything between becomes an equation: on one summary that made a single 5,000-character span covering half a chapter. Pandoc's delimiter rule settles it, but only if an ESCAPED dollar is not allowed to close a span, which is the mistake that turned 5 refusals across the corpus into 24 in one run.

**Seen.** 99 of 248 documents. Operations and Supply Chain, Accounting, Intermediate Accounting.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `currency >0`

### An accounting summary, which is mostly tables

<a id="accounting-tables"></a>

**What it is for.** Journal entries, ledgers and trial balances are tables, and a summary of them is a document made of tables with prose between.

**How to handle it.** Converts to GitHub-flavoured Markdown tables. A journal entry is Account / Debit / Credit and stays that way; the layout phase has element types for these and must not invent its own.

**What goes wrong.** A cell holds ONE line: a newline in it ends the table, and an unescaped pipe opens a column that is not there. Merged cells make rows of different widths, and a separator row narrower than the header silently drops every column past it.

**Seen.** 147 of 248 documents carry tables at all. Summary_Intermediate_Accounting: 154 tables. SUMMARY_Accounting: 91.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `tables >50`

### A PDF wearing a .docx extension

<a id="docx-that-is-a-pdf"></a>

**What it is for.** Usually a summary somebody exported to PDF and renamed, hoping it would be accepted.

**How to handle it.** Refused at preflight on the magic bytes. Go and find the Word file it came from.

**What goes wrong.** Two of four files on one real upload were this. It is common enough to check every time.

**Seen.** SUMMARY_IHC_(GradeGuru).docx, in four places in the catalogue. Social_Psychology_Lectures_EN.docx.

**Recognised by.** `ext = .docx`, `kind = pdf`

### A Word file wearing a .pdf extension

<a id="pdf-that-is-a-docx"></a>

**What it is for.** Somebody renamed it, or a download went wrong. This one is GOOD NEWS: the file is better than its name.

**How to handle it.** Rename it and convert it normally. Do not discard it as a PDF, which is what a rule keyed on the extension does.

**What goes wrong.** The pipeline refuses PDF as a source, so the extension alone decided these were unusable. They are Word documents.

**Seen.** 10 files. Among them 2019-20 Exam.pdf and 2023-24 Exam.pdf, sitting in a live course workspace as past exams, and SUMMARY(Preview)_IHC_(GradeGuru).pdf.

**Recognised by.** `ext = .pdf`, `kind = zip`

### A photograph wearing a .docx extension

<a id="docx-that-is-a-photograph"></a>

**What it is for.** None. A file was renamed, or a download went wrong. It is not the document anybody meant to send.

**How to handle it.** Refused at preflight on the magic bytes. Go and find the real file; there is nothing to salvage.

**What goes wrong.** The extension is not evidence, and neither is the size: 32 KB is a plausible size for a short document.

**Seen.** IBA1_IB_Literature_Summary.docx, 32 KB, JPEG magic.

**Recognised by.** `ext = .docx`, `kind = jpeg`

### A note somebody left instead of the file

<a id="placeholder-note"></a>

**What it is for.** A person told you something and the filesystem swallowed it. The file is a sentence.

**How to handle it.** Read it. It is an answer to a question about the course, not an input.

**What goes wrong.** It is named like a past exam and sits in a folder of past exams. Nothing but opening it says otherwise.

**Seen.** 2020-21 Exam.pdf, in a live course workspace, whose entire contents are: Not gonna do a summary for this.

**Recognised by.** `kind = text`, `kb <2`

### An image that is not the format it claims

<a id="image-mislabelled"></a>

**What it is for.** A screenshot. A phone or an operating system saved PNG bytes under a .jpg name, or something re-encoded it on the way.

**How to handle it.** Harmless for a figure, because the bytes are read and not the name. It matters when a tool picks an encoder by extension.

**What goes wrong.** Listed because the same mistake at document scale is the expensive one, and because it proves the rename happens by accident and not by intent.

**Seen.** 17 files, all named IMG_NNNN.jpg and all PNG.

**Recognised by.** `ext = .jpg`, `kind = png`

## Partly handled

### Word with no styles at all

<a id="word-no-styles"></a>

**What it is for.** Usually a Google Docs export, sometimes a document somebody typed without ever touching the style menu. Either way the heading level exists only as a font size.

**How to handle it.** docx2.js, NOT docx.js, and then LOOK at the result. It ranks the distinct font sizes above the body size into levels, which is typography and not structure.

**What goes wrong.** docx.js does not fail on these; it used to flatten the document to one level in silence, and nothing downstream could tell that from a document that genuinely has no headings. It now exits non-zero and says so.

**Seen.** 35 of 248 Word documents carry no pStyle. Most are short notes; the substantial ones are Questions tutorial C (178 paragraphs), RoughTimeLine (165) and Assg1 draft (104).

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `headingStyles = 0`, `paragraphs >=40`

### Word, exported from Google Docs

<a id="google-docs-export"></a>

**What it is for.** The author wrote it in Google Docs and downloaded it as Word. Common, because Docs is what a laptop already has.

**How to handle it.** Whether docx.js works depends on the document: Docs writes real heading styles when the author used its own heading menu, and nothing when they only made the text bigger. Run docx.js and believe what it reports.

**What goes wrong.** An absent generator is a better signal than a missing style: Word ALWAYS writes one, so its absence means the file came from somewhere else, whatever the rest of it looks like.

**Seen.** 33 of 248 Word documents set no <Application> in docProps/app.xml, which Word always sets. Nevtelen dokumentum.docx is a Docs document that was never even named.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `generator = `

### PDF with a real text layer

<a id="pdf-text"></a>

**What it is for.** Course manuals, past exams, answer keys, grading schemes, tutorial sheets. Almost everything a university publishes that is not the summary itself.

**How to handle it.** Readable, and refused as a SOURCE for a summary. It is an input to Analyze and a checklist item, not something to convert into a lesson.

**What goes wrong.** The PDF extractor needs four hand-tuned parameters per document (font map, page list, size map, footer pattern) and none can be guessed. It is not a general reader and must never be offered as one.

**Seen.** 1,131 PDFs in the census. 24 past exams and answer keys, two course manuals, eight tutorial sheets, four grading schemes.

**Recognised by.** `kind = pdf`, `textLayer = true`

### A PDF a lecturer made in LaTeX

<a id="pdf-latex"></a>

**What it is for.** Problem sets, lecture notes and exams from a mathematics or economics department. The most carefully typeset thing in the course and the hardest to read back.

**How to handle it.** Text extraction works, and the maths does not: LaTeX-made PDFs draw formulas as positioned glyphs, so an integral comes out as scattered letters. Retype the formulas from the rendered page; never trust the extracted text for them.

**What goes wrong.** The prose extracts beautifully, which makes it look as though the whole document did.

**Seen.** 36 PDFs from pdfTeX, plus 7 from dvips and Ghostscript together.

**Recognised by.** `kind = pdf`, `pdfProducer ~pdfTeX`

### A PDF somebody printed from Word

<a id="pdf-from-word"></a>

**What it is for.** The summary, exported. It is the same document as the .docx, one generation later and with everything structural removed.

**How to handle it.** Refused as a source. GO AND FIND THE .docx: it exists, somebody made this from it, and it carries the headings, the numbering and the equations that this does not.

**What goes wrong.** It is the most tempting wrong answer in the whole intake, because it looks complete and it opens.

**Seen.** 125 PDFs name a Microsoft product as their producer, and 7 more say Microsoft: Print To PDF. Almost every summary in the catalogue sits beside its own PDF twin.

**Recognised by.** `kind = pdf`, `pdfProducer ~Microsoft`

## Not handled

### Word with tracked changes still in it

<a id="word-tracked-changes"></a>

**What it is for.** A document mid-edit, where the file holds both what it said and what it will say.

**How to handle it.** NOT HANDLED. The extractor reads every run, so deleted text comes through as if it were still there and the result is a mix of two drafts. Accept the changes in Word first.

**What goes wrong.** Text inside <w:del> reads exactly like text that was never deleted.

**Seen.** None yet, in 248 Word documents. Listed because the failure is silent and the fix is somebody else's ten seconds.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = word`, `tracked >0`

### A scan with no text layer

<a id="pdf-scan-no-text"></a>

**What it is for.** A photographed or scanned handout, an old exam paper, a whiteboard. Common for anything predating the course's own digital records.

**How to handle it.** NOT HANDLED. There is no OCR in this pipeline. Say so plainly, record it as a missing input, and ask for a digital original.

**What goes wrong.** An empty extract from a scan looks exactly like an empty extract from a broken parse. Detect the absent text layer and say which it is.

**Seen.** 455 PDFs carry no /Producer at all, which is where these live. None has yet been needed as a source.

**Recognised by.** `kind = pdf`, `textLayer = false`

### Lecture slides

<a id="powerpoint"></a>

**What it is for.** What the lecturer actually showed. Often the only statement of what is examinable, and the thing students ask about most.

**How to handle it.** NOT HANDLED. There is no PowerPoint reader here. Slides are an input to Analyze, read by a person, and never a source of record.

**What goes wrong.** A deck is not prose and would not become one: its structure is one idea per slide with the argument in the speaker's mouth. Converting it would produce something that reads like a summary and is not one.

**Seen.** 68 .pptx files in the census.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = powerpoint`

### A spreadsheet

<a id="spreadsheet"></a>

**What it is for.** Grade books, datasets a statistics course works on, financial models an accounting course builds.

**How to handle it.** NOT HANDLED as a source. A dataset a course teaches ON belongs in materials, not in a lesson.

**What goes wrong.** A summary that teaches a spreadsheet writes its formulas as text; see spreadsheet-formulas-as-equations. The spreadsheet itself is a different thing.

**Seen.** 104 .xlsx files in the census.

**Recognised by.** `ooxml = excel`

### The old binary Word format

<a id="legacy-doc"></a>

**What it is for.** Anything written before 2007, or by somebody who never changed the default. Still turns up from university archives.

**How to handle it.** NOT HANDLED. It is a compound OLE file and shares nothing with a .docx. Open it in Word and save as .docx; that conversion is lossless and takes a moment.

**What goes wrong.** It is not a zip, so every tool here fails on it at the first byte, which is at least honest.

**Seen.** None in this census, which is itself worth knowing: .doc has finally gone.

**Recognised by.** `kind = ole`

### An iPhone photograph

<a id="heic-photo"></a>

**What it is for.** A student photographed a whiteboard, a worked solution, or a page of a book.

**How to handle it.** NOT HANDLED. Nothing in this pipeline reads HEIC, and the reader will not serve it. Convert to PNG or JPEG first; macOS Preview does it.

**What goes wrong.** It previews fine on a Mac, so it looks like a working image right up to the upload.

**Seen.** 7 files.

**Recognised by.** `ext = .heic`

### A saved web page

<a id="saved-web-page"></a>

**What it is for.** Somebody archived a page from the university's learning environment, usually because it was about to disappear.

**How to handle it.** NOT HANDLED. Read it in a browser and decide what it is; there is nothing here that parses one.

**What goes wrong.** It is one file containing an entire page and its assets, so its size says nothing about how much content it holds.

**Seen.** 15 files, alongside 34 plain .html.

**Recognised by.** `ext = .mhtml`
